Protesters gathered at the Utah Capitol on Saturday to oppose the massive proposed “Stratos” data center campus planned for Box Elder County — a project backed by investor Kevin O’Leary that has quickly become one of the most controversial development fights in Utah.

The proposed AI campus has raised concerns among residents, environmental advocates, and local officials about water usage, emissions, energy demand, transparency, and long-term impacts on northern Utah communities.

Saturday’s protest followed weeks of packed public meetings, growing public backlash, and a referendum effort launched by opponents challenging local approvals.

Check out sltrib.com to learn more.

📸 by Bethany Baker / The Salt Lake Tribune

Celebrity investor Kevin O'Leary agreed Thursday to cut his proposed Stratos data center in Box Elder County's Hansel Valley from 40,000 acres to 20,000, with the data center buildings themselves capped at no more than half of that smaller footprint. The reversal came after Senate President Stuart Adams, who also chairs the quasi-governmental Military Installation Development Authority steering the project, sent O'Leary a public letter demanding a 75% reduction.

O'Leary, who had earlier insisted he wasn't backing down, told NBC News he had "no choice" but to give in, and that Adams made the demand for political reasons. The concessions include water commitments aimed at the Great Salt Lake, set-asides for open space and wildlife, heat-capture technology, and independent environmental review. A Deseret News-Hinckley Institute poll found bipartisan unease: 53% of Utahns opposed the original project, and nearly 7 in 10 said the economic benefits don't outweigh the cost to natural resources.

Adams is calling the size cut proof that "public engagement matters." It's worth being clear about what actually happened here: residents organized, packed hearings, launched a referendum drive, and absorbed baseless smears about foreign funding—and only then did the powerful start listening. That's not the system working as designed. It's people forcing a system that locked them out to respond.

Box Elder County commissioners in rural northern Utah voted unanimously on May 4, 2026 to approve the "Stratos Project" — a 40,000-acre AI data center campus backed by Shark Tank's Kevin O'Leary, dubbed "Wonder Valley" after his "Mr. Wonderful" persona. At 2.5 times the size of Manhattan, it would consume more than double Utah's entire current electricity usage and increase the state's carbon footprint by 50%. Over 1,000 protesters chanted "Shame! Shame! Shame!" as commissioners quickly exited the room. Residents say they received less than a week's notice before the vote. Turns out, it could create a massive heat island capable of devastating the area’s ecology, said Robert Davies, a physics professor at Utah State University.

“I suspected it would not be good,” Davies said. “What I’ve found is it’s so much worse than I even thought it would be.”

News of the proposed sprawling data complex, dubbed the Stratos Project, became public last month. The project’s boosters say it will likely need 9 gigawatts of energy at full build — more than double the electricity currently used by the entire state of Utah. That energy will likely come from a pipeline carrying natural gas from Wyoming to Nevada, Oregon and California. The project’s developer, “Shark Tank” celebrity Kevin O’Leary, specifically chose Box Elder County’s Hansel Valley to build the complex because the pipeline spans it, state officials have said.

Davies has done some back-of-the-envelope calculations to better understand the shear scale of what’s proposed. And what he’s penciled out so far has him alarmed.

“Nine gigawatts, that’s a number that’s really challenging to get your brain around,” the professor said. ”Communicating the scale has been a real problem.”

The project will actually produce more than 9 gigawatts of energy, Davies explained, because anytime a gadget consumes power, it also produces energy in the form of heat, whether it’s a toaster, a car or a sprawling rack of computer servers.

All the heat the Stratos Project emits will add up to another 7 to 8 gigawatts of energy in the form of waste heat.

Typically, waste heat is generated far from the power plant itself, in homes, businesses or on roads where it dissipates.

But for the Stratos project, it will get dumped into the local environment of Hansel Valley, in the same geographic bowl as the power plant. That actually makes the data complex a 16 gigawatt thermal load project, the “equivalent of about 23 atom bombs worth of energy dumped into this local environment every single day,” Davies said.

The AI boom is facing a fierce rural backlash in Utah.

Hundreds of residents gathered at the State Capitol in Salt Lake City to demand a halt to the Stratos Project, a massive proposed hyperscale data center campus planned for rural Box Elder County near the Great Salt Lake.

The project, backed by celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary, has become a flashpoint in the growing fight over artificial intelligence infrastructure, land use, water rights, and local control.

For many ranchers, farmers, and rural voters, the concern is simple: the project is too big, too fast, and too risky. Critics warn the proposed facility could require enormous amounts of electricity, intensify pressure on water resources, generate heat, and reshape agricultural communities already facing drought and environmental stress.

Supporters argue the development is necessary for America’s AI race and national security competition with China. But opponents say rural communities should not be forced to sacrifice their land, water, and quality of life for billionaire-backed tech expansion.

Now local activists are pushing for a referendum, gathering signatures to put the land-use approvals before voters.

The message from rural Utah is clear: AI may be the future, but communities want a say in who pays the price.

More than 600 people packed the Utah State Capitol this week to push back against a proposed data center the size of a small city — and they say the Great Salt Lake could pay the price.

The project, known as "Wonder Valley" (also called Stratos), would span roughly 40,000 acres in Box Elder County. It's backed by "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary, who has pitched it as a major economic engine that could bring jobs, infrastructure, and billions in investment to northern Utah.

But the residents who rallied at the Capitol have one overriding concern: water. Data centers consume enormous amounts of it for cooling, and the Great Salt Lake has already been shrinking for years. Opponents fear a development this large could draw down the water supply even further and accelerate the lake's decline — a problem that affects air quality, wildlife, and the regional economy.

Supporters of the project argue it could be designed with water-efficient cooling and would deliver long-term economic benefits to a rural part of the state. Backers also point to growing demand for computing power and the chance for Utah to become a hub for it.

For now, the two sides are far apart. The crowd at the Capitol made clear that any project touching the Great Salt Lake's water will face serious public scrutiny before it moves forward.

The proposed "Stratos Project" in Box Elder County, Utah, has become a significant focal point in the national debate over the physical and environmental infrastructure required to sustain the rapidly growing artificial intelligence economy. 

Backed by venture capitalist and Shark Tank investor Kevin O'Leary, the massive 40,000-acre hyperscale data center and energy campus represents an unprecedented leap in industrial digital development. At full buildout, the facility is projected to require up to nine gigawatts of electricity—a staggering amount that exceeds the total energy consumption of the entire state of Utah. 

Because the developers plan to power the facility off-grid via an on-site, natural gas-fired plant connected directly to the Ruby Pipeline, the project’s environmental footprint will be highly concentrated within a localized area.

The thermodynamic scale of the project has drawn intense scrutiny, particularly from climate scientists and local physicists analyzing its potential waste energy. 

Because natural gas turbine power plants operate at a specific thermodynamic efficiency, generating nine gigawatts of electricity simultaneously produces an estimated seven to eight gigawatts of pure waste heat, bringing the campus's total thermal load to roughly 16 gigawatts. 

To put this massive output into perspective, a thermal analysis by Utah State University physicist Dr. Rob Davies notes that this daily energy release is mathematically equivalent to the energy profile of detonating 23 atomic bombs. 

This immense heat would be vented directly into the Hansel Valley, a confined desert basin that naturally acts as an atmospheric bowl, trapping the air and threatening to transform the local microclimate into a permanent "heat island."

Ecologists and local advocacy groups, such as Grow the Flow, have raised serious alarms about how this localized warming could impact a region already grappling with the critical decline of the Great Salt Lake. 

The network of industrial-scale dry-cooling fans required to vent the facility's heat is projected to raise local daytime temperatures by 2°F to 5°F, and spike nighttime temperatures by 8°F to 12°F. 

This sharp increase in nighttime warmth risks suppressing the valley’s natural nightly condensation cycle, a vital source of moisture in an arid environment, which could rapidly accelerate soil drying and vegetation loss. 

While developers defend the project by stating it will utilize closed-loop cooling systems that consume far less water than existing agricultural operations, a fierce legal and political battle has emerged, culminating in a local push for a ballot referendum to reverse the county commission's approval of the massive development.

"After delaying its decision by a week, the three-member Box Elder County Commission voted unanimously Monday to approve the massive energy and data campus backed by Utah’s Military Installation Development Authority and celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary....

"The project, dubbed Stratos by MIDA, will occupy some 40,000 acres centered in Hansel Valley north of the Great Salt Lake. O’Leary will be its lead developer."

A group of Utah residents just decided they're done being ignored — and they're taking the fight to court.

The Alliance for a Better Utah and five Box Elder County residents filed suit Wednesday in Utah's 3rd District Court over the approval of Kevin O'Leary's "Stratos Project" — a sprawling AI data center planned for the rural Hansel Valley. Their core argument is simple but explosive: the people who actually live there were never given a real say.

The lawsuit targets the Military Installation Development Authority, or MIDA — an unelected body that signed off on the project. Plaintiffs say MIDA exercised powers "the Utah Constitution never authorized," approving a development that could reshape residents' water, land, environment, and daily lives without any democratic vote. It also names the Box Elder County Commission, Senate President J. Stuart Adams, and state Sen. Jerry Stevenson.

Here's the part raising eyebrows: Adams and Stevenson are sitting legislators who also serve on the MIDA board. The suit argues that holding both roles may violate Utah's ban on occupying more than one office of public trust at once — and that it should render the project's approval null and void.

The pressure is already working. O'Leary has conceded to shrinking the original 40,000-acre footprint by roughly 75%, committing water to the shrinking Great Salt Lake, and setting aside thousands of acres for open space, wildlife, and farming. But the plaintiffs want the court to throw out the approval entirely and permanently block the plan.

The question now: can a handful of residents stop a billionaire's data center empire — and force their own government to answer for how it got approved?

For weeks, many Utahns felt like the Stratos Project was moving forward at full speed with little chance of slowing down.
